title: The solo climb
summary: Pick a Bronze problem nobody in the house has opened, run the whole protocol on your own from the story to the submit button, and take whatever the grader says.
materials: laptop with Python and the editor installed in week 1
the parent-created USACO account, already signed in
paper and pencil for drawing the farm
field journal and the Maker's Log
a grown-up in the room whose hands stay off the keyboard

figure.alt: The route card never changes: choose the problem, read the story aloud, draw the farm, move it by hand, write the three line plan, count the steps, code and test on the sample, then submit and read the verdict, in that order.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop, all six moves, and today you run every one of them yourself: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix.

Ask: every farm problem so far arrived with something already done for you. In week 2 a grown-up drove the keyboard while you called the moves. Since then the shapes have been named before you met them, so you always knew roughly which tool the story wanted. Today nobody names anything. You get a story you have never read, and the whole question is whether you can find the shape inside it on your own.

Imagine: a route card. Climbers write the route down before they start, in order, because at three in the morning nobody invents a plan. Yours has eight moves and they never change. Choose the problem. Read the story out loud. Draw the farm. Move it by hand. Write the three line plan. Count the steps. Code it and test it on the sample. Submit and read the verdict.

Plan, part one, choosing. A grown-up opens the past contests list on the USACO site and brings up two Bronze problems from months nobody in this house has touched. They do not tell you which one is easier, because a route somebody steered you onto is not a route you chose. You read both stories out loud, then pick the one you can already half draw. That is how climbers choose a line: by what they can see from the bottom.

Plan, part two, the rule about the grown-up. Their hands stay off the keyboard for the whole hour. They may do exactly three things: sit nearby, work the account and the submit button if the site needs a grown-up, and hold you to the turnaround. They do not read the problem for you, they do not spot your bug, and if you ask them what to type, the honest answer today is that they do not know.

Plan, part three, the turnaround, decided now while you are calm. After the first rejection you get three honest fixes. Each one is a real change with a reason you can say out loud, tested on the sample before it goes anywhere near the grader. If the third fix does not do it, you stop and write it up. That is not a clock and there is no timer anywhere near this hour. It is a count, agreed before you start, exactly the way an expedition agrees a turnaround before summit day.

And the thing worth being clear about before you begin. Accepted is a summit. A rejection you can explain in your own words, with the failing test named and the fixes written down, is a summit reached in weather: you went up, the mountain gave you what it gave you, and you came back with an honest account of it. The only outcome that is not a climb is the one where nothing gets written down.

Five minutes, hands on the home row, eyes off your fingers. Today's words are the ones a fresh Bronze program always needs: input, int, split, range, for, if, else, print, open, close.

Then these two lines, three times each, landing every colon and every bracket:

n = int(input())

parts = input().split()

steps.title: The paper half, done alone
steps.body:
The laptop stays shut until the last line of this step is finished. That is not a punishment. It is the fastest route up.

Choose. Two stories, read both out loud, pick the one you can half draw already. Say out loud why you picked it, in one sentence, and write that sentence at the top of the page. If halfway through you discover you picked the harder one, that is fine and you do not swap; every climber has been on that ridge.

Read it properly. The whole problem out loud, to a person, in a normal voice. All of it, including the dull part at the end about where the input comes from and where the answer goes, because that dull part is where good solutions die. If you cannot say a sentence out loud without stumbling, you have not understood it yet, so read that sentence again.

Draw the farm. Cows, buckets, fields, stalls, whatever the story has, drawn as boxes and circles with the problem's own numbers written on them. The sample input from the problem page is your drawing's numbers. Copy them exactly.

Move it by hand. Take the sample and walk the story through with a pencil for the first two or three steps, crossing out and rewriting as things change. Then finish it by hand and check that you land on the sample answer the page prints. If your pencil cannot get the sample answer, no program you write today is going to get it either, and finding that out on paper costs you four minutes instead of forty.

Write the three line plan. What the program reads. What it does over and over. What it prints at the end. Three lines, in that order, no code.

Count the steps. The problem page states the biggest sizes it will ever hand you. Take the biggest one and say out loud how many times your loop would run, then whether a laptop finishes that before dinner. You have counted the tries before every run since the pricing simulator, and today is the first time the number came from somebody else's page instead of your own table.

Last line: write your prediction in the field journal. What verdict do you expect, and which test do you think will catch you if one does.
checklist: I chose the problem myself after reading two stories out loud, and nobody told me which was easier
The farm is drawn on paper with the problem's own sample numbers on it
I got the sample answer by hand, with a pencil, before the laptop was opened
My plan is three lines and says what the program reads, repeats and prints
I said out loud how many steps the loop takes at the biggest size the page allows

figure.alt: Air cools about 6.5 C per 1000 metres climbed, and morning ground heat builds clouds through the day into afternoon storms. A dark 1 to 2 am start puts the summit and most of the descent before the storm builds, with the turnaround fixed before anyone leaves the tent.

steps.title: Weather windows, and why summit day starts in the dark
steps.body:
Expeditions do not leave for the top at a sensible hour. They leave at one or two in the morning, in the cold and the dark, and there is real weather behind that choice.

Air cools as it climbs. On an ordinary day it drops about six and a half degrees Celsius for every thousand metres you go up, which is why a mountain can hold snow above a valley full of grass. The sun heats the ground, the ground heats the air lying on it, and that warmed air rises. Rising air cools, the water in it turns to cloud, and on a fine morning those clouds keep piling upward through the day. By early afternoon they can be towers with thunder and lightning in them, and the highest, most exposed rock in the whole landscape is exactly where you do not want to be standing. So the plan is to be on the summit early and most of the way down before the sky builds. The dark start is the price of the calm morning.

The forecast is the other half. Weather people can see a few days ahead with some confidence and a week ahead with much less, and a weather window is simply a run of days the forecast can see and likes. Expeditions wait for one. They do not argue with it, because arguing with weather is not a thing you can win.

And then the rule the whole business turns on: the turnaround, fixed before anyone leaves the tent. If you are not on top by the agreed point, you go down, even if the summit is close enough to touch. It is decided early because it has to be decided by the calm version of you, not the tired one standing in the snow who wants it very badly. Most accidents happen on the way down after a late summit, and turning around on time is the most professional thing anybody does up there.

Your turnaround today is a count, not a clock: three honest fixes after a rejection, then you stop and write it up. The problem will still be there tomorrow. So will the grader.

figure.alt: Air pressure falls by about 1 hectopascal for every 8 metres climbed, starting near 1013 hPa at sea level. A barometer reading that keeps dropping over a few hours warns of a storm system arriving, hours before the clouds or wind change.

steps.title: How a barometer reads the air overhead
steps.body:
The weather window your team waits for is really a pressure story wearing a temperature costume. Air itself has weight, and at sea level that weight presses down with about 1013 hectopascals of pressure, the same unit your kit's barometer reads.

Climb higher and there is less air stacked above you to push down, so the number falls. Near sea level it drops by roughly 1 hectopascal for every 8 metres you climb, though the drop slows further up.

A falling reading over a few hours, even before the wind or the clouds change, is one of the oldest weather warnings there is. Sailors and climbers have trusted a dropping barometer for centuries, because falling pressure usually means a storm system is arriving.

Watch your kit's barometer for a day. A steady reading is a fair-weather clue. A number that keeps dropping is the sky's own warning, hours ahead of the clouds.

figure.alt: Three common line shapes and how a Bronze program reads each: one number alone with int(input()), several numbers with input().split(), and n more lines with a for loop; the plan's own line goes inside that loop, and the print happens only after it ends.

items.label: n more lines: for i in range(n):

steps.title: The climb: code it, test it, submit it
steps.body:
Open the laptop. New file in the season folder git has been watching since week 1, named after the problem, saved before you type anything else.

First, where the input comes from, because the problem page decides this and not you. Recent past problems hand your program its input the ordinary way and read whatever you print. Older ones name two files instead, one to read and one to write, and the page tells you the exact names. If your page names files, the shape is this and the names are its names, not these:

fin = open('problem.in')
fout = open('problem.out', 'w')

and at the end the answer goes out with

fout.write(str(answer) + '\n')
fout.close()

because on a file problem the grader reads problem.out and nothing else, so anything you print goes nowhere. Read the page twice. A correct program that puts its answer in the wrong place is rejected, and it is the most common way a good solution fails.

The three lines that start almost every Bronze program. When a line holds one number on its own, n = int(input()) reads it. When a line holds several numbers with spaces between them, parts = input().split() cuts it into pieces and int(parts[0]) turns the first piece into a number. When the page says n more lines follow, for i in range(n): walks them one at a time. Then your plan's middle line goes inside that loop, and the print goes after it, at the left edge, outside the loop, because an answer printed before the last line has been read is a guess.

Test on the sample before you even think about the grader. Run the program and type the sample input in by hand, line by line, exactly as the page prints it. Then hold your output next to the page's answer and compare it character by character. Not nearly. A missing space, an extra blank line, or the word answer sitting in front of the number is the whole difference between accepted and not.

Submit it yourself. Choose Python as the language, send the file, and then read every test's result, not just the first one. The grader runs your program on secret tests it never showed you, one after another, and reports what happened on each.

Then the verdict, out loud, whatever it says. If it is accepted, write down the part of your own program you were least sure of, because that is the part that got away with something. If it is not accepted, name the failing test and copy the message down word for word before you touch a single line. Then one honest fix at a time, re-tested on the sample after each, three of them, and then you stop. Either way the log gets the true story tonight, including the bit where you were stuck and did not know what to do.
checklist: The program matched the sample exactly, character for character, before anything was submitted
I followed the problem page's own instructions about where the input comes from and where the answer goes
I pressed submit myself and read every test's result, not only the first one
The verdict is written down in my own words, accepted or not
If it was rejected I named the failing test and made my fixes one at a time, stopping at three

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line for each thing that did not work the first time, and what you tried. Today's usual suspects, with the words Python actually uses, because reading the message beats guessing at it.

EOFError: EOF when reading a line. Your program asked for another line and there was not one. Usually the loop runs one time too many, or an input() got left in from an earlier draft.

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10, followed by the text it choked on. Two numbers arrived on one line and you handed the whole line to int() instead of splitting it first.

IndexError: list index out of range. You split a line and then asked for a piece that is not there, usually parts[1] on a line that holds only one number.

An answer that is right and still rejected. Extra words around it, a missing newline, or the answer printed to the screen when the page asked for a file. The grader compares character by character and has no idea what you meant.

A program that is right and still fails the big tests. It works on the sample and runs out of time on the secret ones, which is what counting the steps was for. Write down what you counted and what the page allowed.

And the one that is not a bug: the sample answer and your answer differing in the last decimal place because of how a computer stores fractions. If the problem is about whole things, keep whole numbers all the way through and the question never comes up.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of the paper half: the farm drawn, the sample worked by hand, the three line plan and your written prediction. Then your Python, pasted or as a share link. Then a photo of the verdict screen, whatever it says, with the failing test in shot if there was one.
